transcript:
Header: 2027-03-05 14:30 UTC | Duration: 55m | Attendees: Alex (Redwood AE), Priya (Redwood SE), Jonah (Redwood CSM), Sam (Apollo Eng), Maya (Apollo Product), Leo (Apollo Platform), Nina (Apollo Security)

Summary: quick scoping to align on latency/throughput SLOs for a 4-week POC. Focus on TTFT vs TPOT, p95/p99 targets, measurement plan, workload sizing, and timeline.

00:00 Alex (Redwood): hey everyone, thanks for joining. quick intros?
00:06 Sam (Apollo): Sam here, eng manager, we own the recommendation API, hi.
00:09 Maya (Apollo): Maya, product, we'll be evaluating impact on user experience.
00:12 Alex (Redwood): great, i'll kick off with what we typically measure — TTFT and TPOT — and then priya will talk benchmarks and tooling.
00:18 Priya (Redwood): hi all — yes, TTFT (time to first token) and TPOT (time per token) are the two axes we use. TTFT captures cold start latency and first-token overhead, TPOT captures steady-state throughput/latency per additional token.
00:30 Leo (Apollo): when you say cold start, do you mean container spin-up or model KV-cache misses, or both?
00:35 Priya (Redwood): both — we separate warm vs cold in measurements. cold = model instance not warmed / cold KV cache; warm = recent requests that hit prefix cache and have model weights loaded. we usually report p50/p95/p99 for both windows.
00:46 Maya (Apollo): what percentiles should we expect you to measure? our product team cares about p95 mainly, ops wants p99 for SLOs.
00:52 Priya (Redwood): common pattern: TTFT p95 <= 200ms, p99 <= 400ms for small models on dedicated infra; TPOT p95 <= 25ms/token, p99 <= 60ms/token — but that's highly dependent on model size, hardware (A100/H100), quantization, and batching. these are starting benchmarks, not guarantees.
01:09 Sam (Apollo): that aligns roughly with our goals. our target is p95 end-user latency under 400ms for typical prompt (avg 40 tokens response) and p99 under 1s. we also care about tail for spikes.
01:20 Alex (Redwood): OK so to translate, if TPOT p95 is 25ms/token and average response length is 40 tokens, token time adds ~1s — wait that seems high, yes so TTFT needs to be considered; often we optimize batching to lower per-token and use KV cache to reduce effective tokens. we should model typical prompt lengths.
01:34 Priya (Redwood): right — also note TPOT is influenced by batching and model parallelism. for interactive SLOs we usually size dedicated capacity to meet per-request latency at target concurrency.
01:45 Leo (Apollo): we have a concurrency pattern of bursts to 600 rps for search-like workloads, but average sustained is 120 rps. our median response length is 35 tokens, 95th is 120 tokens.
01:58 Priya (Redwood): perfect, that's the profile we need. for a POC we'll run two types of tests: synthetic open-loop load to validate TPOT under concurrency, and replay of recorded traffic (closed-loop) to validate real-world behavior and autoscaling.
02:12 Maya (Apollo): what about model variants? we're considering a 7B and a 13B quantized model, and possibly a smaller distilled model for fallback.
02:19 Alex (Redwood): good — our plan: baseline both models in hosted sandbox, measure TTFT warm/cold, TPOT at varying batch sizes (1..8), and then run concurrency sweeps to p95/p99. we'll also test a fallback policy to a smaller model when latency breaches.
02:31 Nina (Apollo): security question: if we use Redwood Private in our VPC, does TTFT change because of network latency? also KMS for keys?
02:38 Jonah (Redwood): yes, private deployment can add a small network RTT depending on region and VPC config; we'll measure end-to-end from your app location. KMS/HSM supported — we'll share the whitelist.
02:47 Sam (Apollo): can you quantify instrumentation? we need to be able to attribute p99 spikes to either queueing, batching, or model-level overhead.
02:53 Priya (Redwood): we provide per-request tracing: split times for routing, model load, kv-cache hit/miss, decode per-token time. we'll include a sample tracing output in the benchmark report. note: perf traces can be noisy on early runs.
03:07 Maya (Apollo): measurement window — how long do you run each test to get stable p99 readings?
03:11 Priya (Redwood): for p99 we recommend at least 30 minutes per steady-state load level to capture enough tail events; for cold-start experiments we run repeated cold cycles (boot, single request) across 50 iterations to get variance. for burst tests we run 10-15 minute bursts with ramp up.
03:26 Alex (Redwood): and for success criteria — what does Apollo need to consider pass/fail for the POC?
03:30 Maya (Apollo): product: p95 latency for typical prompts < 400ms (end-to-end), p99 < 1s. engineering: stable throughput to 600 rps burst with graceful degradation and fallback. security: no data egress, KMS ok.
03:41 Sam (Apollo): ops: observe no sustained CPU/GPU saturation beyond defined limits, autoscaling should bring additional capacity within X minutes.
03:48 Priya (Redwood): we'll propose specific numeric SLOs for the POC report: TTFT warm p95 <= 150ms, TTFT cold p95 <= 450ms; TPOT p95 <= 20ms/token, p99 <= 70ms/token on H100 for 13B quantized; fallback model TPOT p95 <= 12ms/token. those are targets to test to; if we can't meet them we'll identify mitigations (quantization, batch tuning, different kernel selection).
04:12 Leo (Apollo): network egress costs are a concern — if batching reduces tokens cost, it might also increase latency; trade-offs?
04:18 Alex (Redwood): exactly — batching helps throughput and cost but increases per-request latency if you wait to fill batches. we can use dynamic batching with SLO-aware timers: small holds to form batches but prioritize latency for interactive traffic. we'll show a config that keeps p95 under target while improving cost.
04:35 Priya (Redwood): measurement plan steps (high level): 1) get sample traffic and prompts from Apollo, 2) run unit microbenchmarks for TTFT/TPOT on candidate infra (H100/A100), 3) run concurrency sweeps (closed and open loop), 4) replay production-like traffic to validate autoscaling and fallbacks, 5) produce report with recommendations.
04:56 Maya (Apollo): timeline? we'd like a 4 week POC. what's realistic?
04:59 Alex (Redwood): typical is 3-6 weeks. proposed: week 0 (this week) align on scope and traffic, week 1 run microbenchmarks and baseline one model, week 2 run load tests and rework configs, week 3 run replay and finalize report; optional week 4 iterate on mitigation and tune for cost.
05:16 Sam (Apollo): what about TTFT variance from cold starts during low traffic windows — could that affect user experience? we can't have spikes during onboarding flows.
05:22 Priya (Redwood): we'll include cold-start guardrails: keep a minimum warm pool for sensitive routes, or use long-lived instances, both increase cost but reduce cold TTFT. we'll model cost/latency tradeoffs in the report.
05:34 Nina (Apollo): on security — can we run POC in our VPC with private endpoints? we need SOC2 and an NDA.
05:40 Alex (Redwood): yes, Private deployment option exists; for POC we can do hosted sandbox then transition to a Private sandbox if you need network isolation. we'll share SOC2 and security docs after call.
05:49 Maya (Apollo): how do you handle synthetic vs real traffic mixes — we expect a heavy tail of long prompts.
05:54 Priya (Redwood): include distribution-driven testing: 70% short(<=40), 20% medium(41-120), 10% long(>120). measure per-bucket p95/p99 and overall end-to-end latency percentiles.
06:08 Sam (Apollo): what metrics do we report besides TTFT/TPOT?
06:11 Priya (Redwood): per-request token counts, queue time, GPU utilization, KV cache hit rate, batch sizes, model occupancy, cost per 1M tokens, and error rates. we'll attach a CSV export and dashboard link.
06:24 Jonah (Redwood): for the POC acceptance we typically ask for: documented SLOs, runbook for observed breaches, and an actioned tuning plan.
06:31 Maya (Apollo): ok let's recap next steps.
06:33 Alex (Redwood): recap: Alex will send benchmark template and pricing, Priya will schedule load test and run initial baselines, Apollo team will send traffic profile and confirm security requirements. we'll aim to start microbenchmarks early next week.
06:45 Sam (Apollo): perfect. thanks.
06:47 Alex (Redwood): thanks everyone, we'll follow up in email with links and calendar invites.

Notes / Measurement Plan (auto-section):
- Workload sizing: use Apollo 7-day histogram; assume avg 120 rps sustained, burst 600 rps. response token distribution: median 35, p95 120. run tests at concurrency levels mapping to rps and average token count.
- Benchmarks: TTFT (cold/warm): 50 cold cycles, 30m warm steady-state. TPOT: batch sizes [1,2,4,8], concurrency sweep [50, 120, 300, 600], measure p50/p95/p99.
- Success criteria (POC pass): end-to-end p95 < 400ms for typical prompts, p99 < 1s; ability to handle 600 rps bursts with fallback path and no data egress incidents.
- Metrics to capture: TTFT (ms), token decode time (ms/token), GPU util (%), batch size distribution, queue time, KV cache hit rate, error rate, cost $/1M tokens.
- Measurement approach: synthetic open-loop for throughput characterization; closed-loop replay for user-experience SLOs and autoscaler exercise. use 30m steady windows for tail stats, repeated cold-start cycles for variance.
- Instrumentation: Redwood tracing + Apollo application-level end-to-end timestamps to attribute network vs model time.
- Timeline: 3-4 weeks suggested: week1 microbenchmarks, week2 load tests, week3 replay and final report, optional week4 tuning.

References: Benchmark template link (sent post-call), security docs link (SOC2, encryption), sample perf trace (attached in follow-up).

End of transcript.
